facts.claim: Dijkstra (1959) sets the problem as points, some pairs joined by a link of known length, and asks for the shortest path between two of them.
Dijkstra (1959) adds points one at a time to the set whose shortest path from the start is known, in order of rising distance, until the goal joins it.
OSRM’s profile docs (checked 2026-10-30) say the shortest and the fastest route are usually different, because speeds differ by type of road, and the route engine prefers the roads that cost least.
Hart, Nilsson and Raphael (1968) prove that A* finds a cheapest path whenever its guess never exceeds the true cost left, and suggest the straight-line distance for cities joined by roads.
Likhachev, Gordon and Thrun (2003) note that multiplying A*’s guess by a factor above 1 often looks at far fewer points, and the path found then costs at most that factor times the cheapest.
Google Maps’ route-planning docs (checked 2026-10-30) ignore current traffic by default, which replies fastest; asked to, the service takes current traffic into account.
OSRM’s traffic docs (checked 2026-10-30) take traffic in as a file of new speeds for stretches of road, which updates those roads’ travel times.
Geisberger and colleagues (2008) tested on a Western Europe road map of about 18 million junctions: about 10 minutes of work ahead of time, then each route question in about 0.2 milliseconds.
Geisberger and colleagues (2008) remove junctions one at a time, least important first, adding a shortcut wherever a removed junction sat on the only quickest path between two others.

OSRM, a route engine built to run on OpenStreetMap maps, offers two ways to prepare a map ahead of time in its README (checked 2026-10-30): contraction hierarchies and Multi-Level Dijkstra, which it recommends by default.
